source_content.content: *Figure 2: An overview of our proposed MR-Search framework. Given a question, the agent first completes an initial episode by interleaving reasoning and tool calls. It then enters an iterative self-reflection loop, where previous episodes serve as experience to inform subsequent searches and answer revisions, enabling iterative improvement across episodes.* ### 3.1 Background Given a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ consisting of question–answer pairs and an external search engine $\mathcal{E}$, our goal is to train a LLM agent to give the answer by iteratively performing reasoning and interacting with $\mathcal{E}$. Many search agent frameworks build upon the ReAct paradigm*(Yao et al., [2022](#bib.bib7 "React: synergizing reasoning and acting in language models"); Jin et al., [2025b](#bib.bib6 "Search-r1: training llms to reason and leverage search engines with reinforcement learning"))*, where agents execute iterative cycles of reasoning and acting until a final answer is reached. When presented with a query, the agent conducts multiple rounds of thought-action-observation sequences. During each round, the RL-based agent $\pi_{\theta}$ formulates a internal Thought ($\tau$) based on the current context, executes a external Action ($\alpha$) such as query, and receives corresponding feedback from search engines as tool Observation ($x$) as shown in Figure[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection for Agentic Search"). The interaction trajectory is denoted as: | | $\displaystyle a\=\left(\tau_{0},\alpha_{0},x_{0},\tau_{1},\alpha_{1},x_{1},\ldots,\tau_{T-1}\right).$ | | (1) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | The first round contains the prompt, while the final round $\tau_{T-1}$ contains only the thought with the final answer $o$, without any further actions. Given this interaction process, we can directly maximize the RL objective with the final outcome rewards to optimize the policy: | | $\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\pi_{\theta})\=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}\big[f_{\text{verifier}}(o,o^{*})\big],$ | | (2) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | where $o$ denotes the final answer extracted from the completed trajectory $a$, $o^{*}$ is the ground-truth answer, and $f_{\text{verifier}}$ represents either a rule-based or model-based verifier. Although agentic search based on outcome rewards has demonstrated promising performance*(Jin et al., [2025b](#bib.bib6 "Search-r1: training llms to reason and leverage search engines with reinforcement learning"); Sun et al., [2025](#bib.bib64 "Zerosearch: incentivize the search capability of llms without searching"); Chen et al., [2025](#bib.bib8 "Learning to reason with search for llms via reinforcement learning"); Shi et al., [2025](#bib.bib37 "Search and refine during think: autonomous retrieval-augmented reasoning of llms"); Wu et al., [2025b](#bib.bib27 "Webdancer: towards autonomous information seeking agency"))*, the outcome rewards are sparse and delayed, leading to ambiguous credit assignment and ineffective search exploration*(Liu et al., [2021](#bib.bib78 "Decoupling exploration and exploitation for meta-reinforcement learning without sacrifices"); Feng et al., [2025](#bib.bib17 "Group-in-group policy optimization for llm agent training"); Wang et al., [2025b](#bib.bib21 "StepSearch: igniting llms search ability via step-wise proximal policy optimization"))*. ### 3.2 Meta-RL Framework for Agentic Search In this section, we introduce MR-Search, a Meta-RL framework for agentic search built on a cross-episode meta training scheme. Each meta-episode is modeled as a sequence of episodes, encouraging early exploration and subsequent exploitation of accumulated context, as shown in Figure[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection for Agentic Search"). By modeling prior episodes in context through a standardized self-reflection paradigm and propagating this information across episodes, MR-Search enables increasingly informed search, leading to broader exploration and reduced redundancy. *Figure 3: We evaluate MR-Search, Search-R1 with sequential reflection inference (Search-R1-S), and Search-R1 with parallel sampling (Search-R1-P), selecting the most frequent answer among the generated trajectories. Shaded regions show the standard deviation across 3 runs. We observe that MR-Search achieves the best performance. See §[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Further Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection for Agentic Search") for details* *Algorithm 1 MR-Search: One Sample Update* 1:Input: policy $\pi_{\theta}$, sample $(x,o^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}$, group size $G$, reflection steps $N$ 2:for $i\=1,\dots,G$ do $\triangleright$ Group of meta-episodes 3:$C\leftarrow x$ $\triangleright$ Initialize context 4: for $n\=0,\dots,N-1$ do $\triangleright$ Inner episodes 5:$a_{i,n}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid C)$ 6:$C\leftarrow C\oplus a_{i,n}\oplus\textsc{Reflect}(C)$ $\triangleright$ Self-reflection 7:$r_{i,n}\leftarrow f(a_{i,n},o^{*})$ $\triangleright$ Reward 8:Compute $A_{i,n}$ via Eq. (7–8) $\triangleright$ RLOO advantage 9:$\theta\leftarrow\textsc{RL\_Update}(\theta,{r_{i,n}})$ with Eq. ([9](#S3.E9 "In 3.3 Policy Optimization with Multi-Turn Advantages ‣ 3 MetaSearch: Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Search ‣ Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection for Agentic Search")) The key motivations are twofold: (i) For LLM agents, model limitations often stem from insufficient exploration within a single trajectory rather than inadequate reasoning capacity*(Shen et al., [2025](#bib.bib55 "Thinking vs. doing: agents that reason by scaling test-time interaction"))*; incorrect answers may consistently appear across multiple samples in parallel, as shown by*Fan et al. ([2025](#bib.bib77 "SSRL: self-search reinforcement learning")); Si et al. ([2026](#bib.bib53 "Towards execution-grounded automated ai research"))*. (ii) LLMs exhibit strong self-reflection capabilities, enabling inference-time adaptation that accumulates information from prior interactions across episodes, naturally leveraging in-context learning mechanisms. As shown in Figure[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Meta-RL Framework for Agentic Search ‣ 3 MetaSearch: Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Search ‣ Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection for Agentic Search"), MR-Search substantially improves over baselines both with sequential reflection and parallel sampling and its performance grows with more turns, suggesting that the ability for self-reflection emerges as models become stronger in-context meta-learners. Given an input question, the search agent $\pi_{\theta}$ first generates the first episode, in which it interacts with external tools until reaching the final answer, following the procedure in §[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Background ‣ 3 MetaSearch: Meta-Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Search ‣ Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection for Agentic Search"). | | $\displaystyle{a}_{0}\sim\pi_{\theta}({a}).$ | | (3) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | Unlike standard RL-based search agents*(Jin et al., [2025b](#bib.bib6 "Search-r1: training llms to reason and leverage search engines with reinforcement learning"); Song et al., [2025](#bib.bib22 "R1-searcher: incentivizing the search capability in llms via reinforcement learning"))*, where episodes are independent, MR-Search conditions each episode on the preceding one. After each episode, the search agent invokes the tool to iteratively improve its answer under the self-reflection paradigm. Specifically, given an initial episode, we apply a reflection prompt (Appendix[A.1.3](#A1.SS1.SSS3 "A.1.3 The Details of Implementation ‣ A.1 Experimental Details ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Self-Reflection for Agentic Search")) that triggers the model to refine its answer by conditioning on previous episodes as context and producing an additional episode with another answer. | | $\displaystyle a_{1}\sim p_{\theta}({a}_{1}\mid{a}_{0}),~~{a}_{2}\sim p_{\theta}({a}_{2}\mid a_{0},a_{1})\dots$ | | (4) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | By repeating the multi-turn self-reflection process $N-1$ times, in MR-Search, each meta-episode consists of $N$ episodes sequentially generated by the search agent: | | $\displaystyle y\=(a_{0},a_{1},\cdots,a_{N}),$ | | (5) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | where we can compute rewards independently for each episode $a$ using the answer $y_{n}$ extracted from the $n$th episode by the verifier.
